analysis.one_liner: Requires online disclosure of campaign money, moves enforcement to the Justice Department, raises contribution limits, and ends presidential public financing.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced in January 1999 and never received a vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made campaign money easier to see: political committees would have to file electronically, the Federal Election Commission would have to post reports online within 24 hours, and anyone spending $100,000 or more on ads that mention federal candidates would have to disclose it within 24 hours. It would also raise contribution limits by adjusting them for inflation, give taxpayers a credit of up to $200 ($400 for couples) for political contributions, end the taxpayer checkoff that publicly finances presidential campaigns, and move enforcement of campaign finance law from the FEC to an office under the Attorney General.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want to see who is paying for campaign advertising, since issue-advocacy spending and corporate and union political activity would have to be disclosed quickly and posted online. Small-dollar donors would get a tax credit for half of what they give, up to $200 per person. Big donors would also benefit, because contribution limits would rise with inflation from their 1974 levels.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters seeking disclosure; donors via tax credits

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FEC to make all campaign finance reports available on the Internet within 24 hours of receipt and makes electronic filing mandatory rather than optional.
Requires anyone paying $100,000 or more for a communication that names or shows a federal officeholder or candidate, or mentions a national party, to report the payment to the FEC within 24 hours.
Requires corporations, national banks, and labor unions to disclose to the FEC within 24 hours any year in which they spend $5,000 or more on specified political activities.

Closes the 'best efforts' loophole so political committees can no longer skip identifying donors who give more than $200 a year, and requires 24-hour reporting of contributions made in the final 60 days before an election.
Creates a tax credit for one-half of an individual's political contributions, up to $200 per person or $400 per joint return, effectively refunding part of what small donors give to campaigns.
Publishes the names of candidates whose committees accepted prohibited contributions.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the new contribution tax credit, and the presidential public financing checkoff would end, with leftover funds swept into the Treasury. Presidential candidates would lose access to matching funds and convention financing. Political parties would face new disclosure duties for $250,000-plus non-federal money, and big outside spenders would lose the ability to run candidate-focused ads anonymously.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, presidential candidates, and undisclosed big spenders

drawbacks.text: The bill indexes contribution limits to inflation, which would raise them well above their 1974-era levels and increase the weight of large individual donors in campaigns.

It transfers enforcement of campaign finance law from the FEC to a new office under the Attorney General, a political appointee, and cuts the FEC from six commissioners to two; the Attorney General could also veto FEC regulations, with approval assumed after 90 days of silence.

It terminates the Presidential Election Campaign Fund and the primary matching payment account after 2000, ending the voluntary taxpayer-financed system that lets candidates run without relying on private donations.
The tax credit uses public money to subsidize campaign contributions, a benefit that goes to people who have spare cash to give rather than those who do not.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The disclosure provisions are the strongest part: putting FEC reports online, forcing 24-hour disclosure of six-figure issue-advocacy spending, and closing the donor-identification loophole would have given ordinary voters a far clearer picture of who funds campaigns. But the same bill raises contribution limits, ends public financing of presidential campaigns, and moves enforcement to an office run by a presidential appointee — changes that critics of big money would see as working against the disclosure gains. Whether the bill netted out as reform or as an alternative to stricter reform depends on which provisions you weight most.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever acted on it, and it died without a floor vote when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. David Dreier introduced the bill on January 6, 1999, the opening day of the 106th Congress.
The same day, it was referred to the House Administration, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees.
No committee reported the bill and no vote was ever scheduled; the action record shows no activity beyond the referral.
The bill expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: large donors kept contribution limits at 1974 levels, outside groups could keep spending on candidate-focused issue ads without disclosure, and the FEC kept its enforcement role. Supporters of broader disclosure and of stricter campaign finance overhaul gained nothing from this bill's death, since it never advanced — but the bill also contained provisions (higher limits, an end to public financing) that reform advocates would have opposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big donors and undisclosed outside spenders

for.name: 1 House Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members signed on.

against.name: House Administration, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 6, 1999 and never reported it out for a House vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape cannot be measured; the bill was introduced by a Republican with a single Republican cosponsor and no Democratic support recorded.

industries.industry: Large individual donors and wealthy households
industries.note: Contribution limits would rise with inflation from their 1974 levels, and donors would get a tax credit of up to $200 ($400 joint) for half of what they give. Both changes increase the influence of people with money to donate relative to voters who cannot contribute.

Indexing and the tax credit would boost party fundraising, but parties would have to disclose contributors and disbursements of $250,000 or more in non-federal money — a real loss of anonymity for soft-money channels.

industries.industry: Issue-advocacy advertisers (corporations, unions, and interest groups running candidate-focused ads)
industries.note: Anyone paying $100,000 or more for ads naming federal candidates would have to disclose within 24 hours, and corporations, banks, and unions would disclose $5,000-plus political activity. Their interest in anonymous spending runs against voters' interest in knowing who is paying for the ads they see.
The Presidential Election Campaign Fund and primary matching payments would end after 2000, removing public financing that lets candidates run without relying on large private donations.
